data.title: <![CDATA[EMA Panel Backs Lilly’s Foundayo for Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes in Europe]]>
data.description:
The European Medicines Agency’s Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use has recommended granting marketing authorization in the European Union for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo (orforglipron) for weight management and the treatment of type 2 diabetes in adults, the agency announced Friday. The European Commission, which makes the final approval decision, typically follows CHMP recommendations within a few weeks.

The positive opinion marks a significant milestone in Lilly’s international expansion strategy for orforglipron, which the company has submitted for regulatory review in approximately 40 markets globally. Foundayo received FDA approval for obesity in April 2026 and launched in the United States in the second quarter of the year. An FDA submission for the type 2 diabetes indication in the US is also pending.

What CHMP Evaluated

The CHMP’s recommendation for the weight management indication is based on two studies involving more than 4,740 adults with obesity or overweight. One study enrolled adults without type 2 diabetes who had at least one weight-related health condition, while the other enrolled adults with type 2 diabetes.

data.description: After months of prodding, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and member states of the European Union have begun taking numerous steps to ensure that clinical trial sponsors do a better job of registering their studies and reporting results for public consumption.

data.title: <![CDATA[The Bubble You Don’t Know You’re In: A Three-Part Series on The Medical Benefit Bubble]]>
data.description:
There is a conversation happening in boardrooms and brand planning cycles across the pharmaceutical industry right now, and it goes something like this: “We’re not exposed to the gross-to-net bubble. We’re a medical benefit product. Our pricing is stable. And besides, our orphan designation protects us from negotiation.”

That statement is technically accurate. It is also dangerously incomplete.

Chief commercial officers, brand leads, and pricing strategists who manage physician-administered, infused, and injected products have spent two decades operating under a reimbursement architecture that the government deliberately designed to be stable, transparent, and resistant to the pricing distortions that inflated the pharmacy benefit side of the ledger. For the most part, that architecture worked exactly as intended.

Until now.

A convergence of forces — loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) cycles, biosimilar market dynamics, coverage determination as a pricing mechanism, and the arrival of Maximum Fair Price (MFP) — is introducing structural pressure to the medical benefit space that the industry has never had to model before. The commercial leaders who navigate the next five years most effectively will not be the ones who feel most protected.

They will be the ones who stopped assuming they were protected and started modeling what comes next.

Two Bubbles. Two Completely Different Architectures.

To understand why medical benefit is now under pressure, you first have to understand why the pressure looks nothing like what happened on the pharmacy benefit side. The pharmacy benefit gross-to-net bubble was a creature of pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) economics and how those incentives work against a manufacturer in government markets such as Medicaid, Medicare, 340B, and the Federal Supply Schedule (FSS).

This model in which manufacturers start with a high wholesale acquisition cost (WAC), pay large rebates to PBMs in exchange for formulary placement, continuously raise WAC above the Consumer Price Index, and simply deal with statutory government price implications always had a life expectancy on it. This bubble is easy to see: with LOEs, WAC reductions, and MFP, it is set to rapidly deflate.

Medical benefit pricing, however, was built on an entirely different foundation — one that made that kind of inflation structurally impossible. When Congress enacted the Medicare Modernization Act (MMA) in 2003, it created the Average Sales Price (ASP) methodology, effective 2005, because the government had grown tired of chasing discounts through estimates and surveys.

Rather than negotiate or approximate net prices, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) required manufacturers to report sales prices net of most reportable discounts, rebates, and other price concessions, subject to statutory and regulatory exclusions, and average them across the applicable reporting period. The result was ASP: a market-derived, quarterly reported price that became the basis for Medicare Part B reimbursement at ASP plus 6%.

The discipline the system imposed was elegant in its logic. The goal of every well-managed medical benefit brand became — and remains — to keep WAC and ASP as close to a 1:1 ratio as possible.

Reportable discounts and price concessions extended through the channel — including to specialty clinics, hospitals, group purchasing organizations (GPOs), and distributors — flow into the ASP calculation and reduce future Medicare reimbursement, generally with a two-quarter sales-to-payment lag. Discounts were not free in this system.

They carried a systemic cost that showed up in the reimbursement statements of every infusion center and oncology practice in the country. Clinics track ASP changes with the same precision that manufacturers track gross-to-net erosion on the pharmacy side — because a meaningful ASP move changes both their cost of goods and their reimbursement margin simultaneously.

Although this was the invention of the federal government, policy makers have increasingly challenged the pricing outcomes that developed under it. The response from industry was not simply to lay down and take it.

Rather, manufacturers increasingly launched at prices closer to the point at which products historically might have ended their lifecycles. Traditional Medicare did not have direct price-negotiation authority, and it does not generally manage physician-administered drugs through PBM-style formularies, rebate-driven preferred positioning, or step therapy.

Coverage instead operates through the reasonable-and-necessary standard, National and Local Coverage Determinations, and related Medicare coverage policy; Medicare Advantage plans have additional utilization-management tools. Consequently, our industry saw launch prices of medical benefit products jump from roughly $40,000/year when MMA went into effect to more than $150,000/year in 2026.

data.title: <![CDATA[Domestic Manufacturing Is a Meaningful But Incomplete Answer]]>
data.description:
Drug shortages remain a difficult to fix issue for the pharma industry and are an issue that can have devastating results. Often times, shortages hit because of an increased demand for the medication, leaving patients waiting for gaps in the supply chain to be filled.

Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with Marc Wagner, an FDA and life sciences attorney at Fox Rothschild, about the manufacturing and regulatory pressures that contribute to drug shortages. According to him, these shortages happen for a variety of reasons and there is single fix.

Instead, there are multiple steps the industry must take to prepare for increases in demand and pipeline disruptions. A major issue is the industry’s dependence on overseas production, which leaves the supply open to global pressures. According to Wagner, a majority of generic drug products are manufactured outside of the US, meaning that these sites may not be unable to pick the slack.

Click for the video version of this interview!

Pharmaceutical Executive: What manufacturing issues continue to contribute to drug shortages?
Marc Wagner: Drug shortages are a multifactorial systems failure driven by many different factors — overseas dependencies, manufacturer incentives including pricing and reimbursement, and regulatory burdens among them. But to directly answer the question of why manufacturing issues contribute to drug shortages, I think we first need to take a step back and define what a drug shortage actually is, because that definition shapes everything we see in the drug shortage marketplace.

The answer largely depends on who you ask. The FDA maintains its own definition of a drug shortage — and as of today, the FDA lists 70 drugs as currently in shortage. The American Society of Health-System Pharmacists tracks drug shortages separately, and according to their metrics, the number is 188. That is a dramatic difference — one organization is reporting more than twice as many shortages as the other. Getting clear on the definition is therefore critical to understanding the dynamics and the true scope of the problem.

As for the manufacturing issues that contribute to shortages: quality control failures are a significant driver. But compounding that, as I mentioned, is our dependence on overseas sources for raw materials, active pharmaceutical ingredients, and in some cases finished dosage products. Complex global supply chains, combined with manufacturing quality challenges, can all converge to create or worsen drug shortages.

data.title: <![CDATA[AstraZeneca Taps insitro AI for MASH in Deal Worth Up to $1.5 Billion]]>
data.description:
AstraZeneca has signed a drug discovery collaboration and licensing agreement with insitro to apply artificial intelligence (AI) to target identification and therapeutic design in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and cardiomyopathies, the companies announced Oct. 15.1,2 Insitro will receive $40 million upfront and is eligible for up to approximately $1.46 billion in milestones.1,2

Sharon Barr, executive vice president and head of BioPharmaceuticals research and development at AstraZeneca, tied the agreement to target selection: “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximizing the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”1

What are AstraZeneca and insitro agreeing to do?

Insitro will use its Virtual Human platform to identify causal disease biology in both indications and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development candidate.1,2 The platform combines large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design.1

AstraZeneca will take the clinical development and regulatory work and holds exclusive worldwide rights to the selected programs; insitro’s release adds that AstraZeneca will also lead commercialization.1,2

Beyond the upfront payment, insitro is eligible for single-digit royalties on global sales.1,2 The two releases describe the milestones slightly differently: AstraZeneca cites development and commercial milestones, while insitro includes discovery milestones.1,2

The upfront payment represents less than 3% of the combined headline value, and neither company disclosed the number of targets, program timelines or payment schedule.

Why are MASH and cardiomyopathies difficult to treat?

Insitro’s release says each disease is defined by heterogeneity, with a single diagnostic label covering patients whose underlying biology differs, which has complicated treatment.2

From time to time over the past couple of years, we have taken a pulse check, chronicled right here, on artificial intelligence (AI), noting how its connections across biopharma seem to be everywhere — and growing. Consider this another check-in. Only now, the conversation feels different.

As three guest pieces in our October issue of Pharmaceutical Executive illustrate, the question is becoming less about what AI can do and more about what it should do. And, going a step further, what needs to surround AI to create meaningful value across life sciences and health care.

data.title: <![CDATA[When Experience, Evidence, and AI Disagree in Pharma, What Should Leaders Do?]]>
data.description:
Three Answers. One Decision.

Consider a hypothetical launch review, six months before anticipated approval. The clinical profile is promising, the market is attractive, and expectations are rising.

Yet payer access is unresolved, competitor moves remain uncertain, and patient persistence is still an assumption. Leadership must commit resources anyway.

The commercial leader wants to move aggressively. Experience suggests that underinvesting at launch could leave the company struggling to catch up.

The analytics team sees a narrower early opportunity. Its scenarios suggest concentrating resources on patients most likely to gain access and start treatment.

Then an AI-assisted analysis arrives. Using available claims patterns, payer signals, patient journeys, and launch analogs, it points somewhere else: the biggest constraint may not be awareness; it may be access and persistence.

If that interpretation holds, the next dollar of promotion could create less value than the next dollar invested in payer evidence or patient services. Three credible answers and one decision.

The scene is hypothetical, but it illustrates a dilemma that also arises in portfolio reviews, market-access investments, and resource allocation. Pharma executives have always made consequential decisions before they knew all the facts.

Now AI adds another source of interpretation, often quickly and with persuasive confidence. The executive challenge is to understand what each source contributes, where each can fail, and which assumption should determine the next commitment.

System 1: Experience Sees the Pattern

Daniel Kahneman’s distinction between fast, intuitive thinking and slower, deliberate reasoning offers a useful starting point. System 1 is fast and driven by pattern recognition.

In pharma, an experienced market-access leader may sense that a value proposition will meet payer resistance, or a commercial leader may recognize an uptake pattern that a forecast overlooks.¹

This judgment has value. Years of experience can reveal context and patterns that a spreadsheet misses.

But experience can also become an anchor. The last successful launch may not be the right analog.

Competitive intensity may have changed and utilization management may be tighter. A familiar market can create false confidence.

The discipline is to expose intuition’s assumptions. Before presenting the forecast or AI recommendation, capture the team’s initial view.

Ask:

  • What do we believe and why?
  • What has to be true for that belief to hold?
  • What evidence would change our mind?

System 1 should start the conversation. It should not end it.

System 2: Evidence Tests the Story

System 2 is slower and deliberate: the work of examining forecasts, segmentation, payer research, patient-flow models, scenarios, and financial analysis. These are modes of reasoning rather than separate departments.

Analysts use intuition, and commercial leaders reason carefully. Its purpose is not simply to add rigor. It is to make the strategy confront evidence.

That distinction matters, as a sophisticated forecast can still be built on an optimistic assumption.

Research can answer the questions the organization chose to ask while missing the question that matters. A polished strategy deck can create confidence without materially improving judgment.

For executives, the test is straightforward: did the analysis challenge the strategy, or merely validate it? If the launch plan assumes rapid adoption, step outside the model.

<![CDATA[The Fundamentals of Omnichannel Still Apply: Q&A with Pat McGloin]]>
data.description:
The pharma and biotech industries are asking the same questions about AI as most other industries: what can it do, and what can it actually do? Over the past two years, the technology has built up a lot of hype over the possibilities.

Now, as people across industries become more experienced with it, they have a better understanding of AI’s abilities. They also understand its limitations much better.

Pharmaceutical Executive spoke with Pat McGloin, chief client officer and life science practice leader at MERGE, about AI’s potential in creating personalized HCP and patient engagement at scale. According to him, generative AI likely isn’t the sole answer for creating these systems while also ensuring regulatory compliance.

Pharmaceutical Executive: What are the dangers of AI hype for pharma?
Pat McGloin: The biggest danger I see is companies feeling pressure from leadership to “get into AI” before they have decided what problems they are trying to solve, what foundation the technology requires, or how it fits into the brand’s overarching strategy. That can create a lot of noise and activity without generating real progress.

Within pharma, I believe AI should operate inside a well-governed, walled-garden environment when possible. By that, I mean a secure and controlled system built on trusted data, approved content, clear access rules and appropriate regulatory oversight. That is especially important in an industry dealing with sensitive health information, complex treatment decisions and strict promotional requirements.

The lesson itself is not new. The same fundamentals we have spent years trying to get right in omnichannel still apply. Start with clean, organized and connected data. Establish a consistent taxonomy. Define what success actually looks like. Then reverse engineer the content, technology, measurement and operating model required to achieve it. Only after that should you determine where AI can amplify the system through greater speed, efficiency, insight or personalization.

The old adage still holds true: garbage in, garbage out. AI can simply process the garbage faster and distribute it at greater scale. If your data is fragmented, your content is disconnected or your objectives are unclear, AI will not rescue the strategy. It will magnify those weaknesses.

The opportunity with AI is real, but AI should support the commercial strategy, not become the strategy. Master the brilliant basics first. Then apply AI where it can make a well-designed system smarter, faster and more responsive without compromising trust, compliance or the human experience.

PE: In what ways is generative AI not capable of creating meaningful personalization?
McGloin: Generative AI can make personalization more precise, but it cannot make it meaningful on its own. At MERGE, we are strong proponents of human-in-the-loop AI. We see it as an executional enabler of connection, but not the source of the human insight that makes that connection feel real.

By now, we have all been exposed to AI slop: the endless stream of content that looks fine at first glance but, on closer inspection, reads like word salad and is instantly forgettable. Patients, caregivers and HCPs do not want or need more of that. No one does, really. People are more strapped for time and attention than ever, while the volume of information competing for that attention continues to grow. If we use generative AI simply to create more content faster, we are adding noise to a system that is already overwhelmed by it.
